name: Avene Thermal Spring Water

card.summary: A low-mineral French spring water used in sprays and skincare to soothe and calm sensitive or irritated skin.

quick.overview:
Avene Thermal Spring Water comes from a spring in the Cevennes mountains of France and is used in sprays and creams for sensitive skin. It is promoted for soothing redness and irritation.

Studies, many run with the hydrotherapy centre or the brand, report benefits in atopic dermatitis and comfort after procedures such as laser resurfacing.
quick.how: Applied as a mist or in moisturizers and cleansers, sometimes alongside acne or procedure aftercare.
quick.risks: Generally reported to be well tolerated; the water is not a treatment on its own for serious skin disease.

lead: Avene Thermal Spring Water is a low-mineral spring water from Avene-les-Bains in southern France, used in a skincare range to soothe sensitive skin.[5][6] People spray or apply it to calm redness, stinging and tightness, including in the days after cosmetic procedures and alongside irritating acne treatments such as topical retinoic acid, so that skin looks and feels calmer and treatment can continue.[7][8] A hydrotherapy centre has treated skin conditions with it since the 1700s, according to Wikipedia and the review literature.[1][6]

Research reviews describe effects of the water on histamine release, inflammation, keratinocyte differentiation and immune cells such as mast cells, dendritic cells and T cells.[1][2][5] Clinical studies cover atopic dermatitis at the hydrotherapy centre and aftercare use, for example with retinoic acid in acne, after laser resurfacing and after photodynamic therapy.[3][7][8][12] Much of this research is associated with the hydrotherapy centre or the brand's owner.[3]

angle.text: People spray or apply it to calm irritated skin, including after procedures or with irritating treatments. Calmer, less red skin is the visible result, and in studies of acne and laser patients it was associated with better tolerance of the underlying treatment.

infobox: Hydrotherapy centre treating chronic skin disease; reopened 1990 [11][3]
Soothing sensitive or irritated skin, post-procedure aftercare

paras: The water rises at the Sainte-Odile spring in Avene-les-Bains, a commune in the Herault department of southern France. Rainwater filters through the Cevennes mountains before resurfacing there, and the water is described as having a low mineral content, which Wikipedia says is thought to make it suitable for sensitive skin.[6][5] The thermal hydrotherapy centre uses it to treat conditions including atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, eczema and burns.[6]

The water is also bottled as a mist and used as a base for moisturisers, cleansers and other products in the Avene skincare range. The brand belongs to Pierre Fabre, the French pharmaceutical and cosmetics group founded in Castres in 1962 by Pierre Fabre; Laboratoires Avene were created in 1989 and the thermal spa reopened in 1990.[11]

Users apply the spray to soothe redness and irritation, to refresh skin and as aftercare following facial procedures. Reviews describe adjunct use for chronic skin disease and tolerance after procedures.[3][5] The idea is that calmer, less irritated skin looks better and tolerates treatments such as retinoids more consistently.[7]

Atopic dermatitis is the most frequent condition treated at the Avene hydrotherapy centre, and children make up a large share of patients.[1] Reviews from the centre also describe a three-week hydrotherapy programme for psoriasis, atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis and its effect on symptoms and quality of life.[10] A therapeutic patient education programme has also been developed at the centre.[4]

In vitro experiments reported in a 2011 review demonstrated effects on membrane fluidity, antiradical and anti-inflammatory properties, effects on mediators of the immune response and a stimulating effect on keratinocyte differentiation.[5] A 2017 review lists effects on histamine release, anti-inflammatory effects in standardised models and immunomodulation of cytokines involved in atopic dermatitis, including interferon, IL-2 and IL-4.[1]
A 2020 review of the water's effects on leucocytes reports that mast cells, dendritic cells and CD4+ T cells are modulated by it, and concluded that the water has a tolerogenic potential.[2]

A review of cohort studies and clinical trials reported improvement in SCORAD (atopic dermatitis severity) and quality-of-life scores, including trials run outside the hydrotherapy centre intended to show a specific effect of the water.[1] A 2020 overview of studies at the centre reported that hydrotherapy was effective as adjuvant management for chronic skin diseases and temporary skin injuries, relieving symptoms with excellent tolerance.[3]

In a randomized, open, multicentre study of 69 people with acne, 34 used a retinoic acid preparation alone and 35 used it with an Avene water spray as needed for 28 days; retinoic acid caused marked irritation in both groups, scaling was significantly lower in the water group, and investigators rated overall tolerance better, while erythema, burning and itching did not differ significantly.[7]

After laser resurfacing, 74 patients were randomized to petrolatum ointment alone or with an Avene spray in an open multicentre trial followed for 84 days. The spray group had significantly less erythema from day 14 onward (with a nonsignificant trend on day 28), less itching on day 28 and less stinging and tightening on days 14 and 21; pain was not changed.[8]

In a double-blind randomized study of 25 patients after photodynamic therapy with 5-ALA, Avene water was compared with a higher-mineral spring water spray. Pain was significantly lower with Avene on days 2, 4 and 7, itching on day 7, while erythema, stinging and tightening did not differ, and 83% of patients wanted to continue the Avene water.[12] A separate comparative study tested Avene water with other topical products around photodynamic therapy and intense pulsed light, and concluded that a topical regimen before or after the procedures can reduce symptoms.[9] A 2026 review of the Avene hydrotherapy experience summarises clinical evidence in inflammatory skin disease and post-procedure complications, based on conference proceedings from physicians and dermatologists.[10]

Clinical overviews describe the water as having excellent tolerance in the studies conducted at the hydrotherapy centre.[3] Marketed spring-water products are sold over the counter. Reviews position the water as adjunctive management rather than a stand-alone treatment for serious skin disease.[3][5]

Much of the clinical research summarised in reviews was conducted at the Avene hydrotherapy centre.[3] The acne and laser trials were open-label (participants knew which treatment they received), while the photodynamic therapy comparison was double-blind.[7][8][12] Wikipedia states that more than 150 biological, pharmacological and clinical studies have been performed, though it does not source the count.[6]

lore.intro: Thermal spring waters are discussed by skincare users as calming mists for sensitive, red or irritated skin, and Avene is among the best-known brands. The claims below summarise how it is described and what published studies report.

claims.claim: The spray soothes redness and irritation.
claims.believers: Users describe using the mist to calm skin and reduce stinging and tightness.
claims.experts: After laser resurfacing, an Avene spray with an emollient was associated with less erythema, itching, stinging and tightening than the emollient alone in a 74-patient open trial [8]. After photodynamic therapy, pain and itching were lower than with a higher-mineral spring water in a 25-patient double-blind study [12].

claims.claim: Using it with retinoids makes acne treatment easier to tolerate.
claims.believers: Users pair the mist with irritating acne treatments to keep using them.
claims.experts: In a 69-patient randomized study, scaling was lower and investigator-rated tolerance better with retinoic acid plus Avene water than with retinoic acid alone, but erythema, burning and itching did not differ significantly [7].

claims.claim: The mineral content makes this water special compared with plain water.
claims.believers: Brand materials and the hydrotherapy centre describe the water as an active component with specific properties [5].
claims.experts: Reviews report effects on keratinocytes, immune cells and mediators in vitro and in clinical comparisons [2][5], while noting that much of the work was conducted at the centre [3]. A comparison against another spring water found differences in pain and itching but not redness after photodynamic therapy [12].

claims.claim: Thermal water helps eczema and atopic dermatitis.
claims.believers: Patients treated at the hydrotherapy centre report relief, and the centre has operated since the 1700s according to reviews [1].
claims.experts: A review of cohort studies and trials reports improvement in SCORAD and quality-of-life scores, with trials outside the centre intended to demonstrate a specific effect of the water [1]. Reviews describe it as adjunct management [3].

claims.claim: It can replace medical treatment for chronic skin disease.
claims.believers: Some users prefer spring-water care to topical drugs.
claims.experts: Reviews describe the water as effective adjuvant management for chronic skin diseases rather than as a stand-alone treatment [3].
